title: 3-Read Friday #65: Motivation, Paper-Folding, and Do Nows
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #65 of 3-Read Friday leads with Carl Hendrick summarizing a new Educational Psychologist paper by Kou Murayama and Luise von Keyserlingk that critiques decades-old motivation theories for describing what motivates students without explaining the underlying mechanism. Paul Rowlandson, whose return to blogging Barton welcomes enthusiastically, shares an extended set of questions teachers can pose while folding paper into geometric shapes, spanning properties of shapes through to KS4 similarity and proof. Dylan Kane closes with his own 'Do Now' routine -- a tightly time-boxed, low-stakes retrieval activity -- offered as Barton's own ongoing Do Now research (via his podcast with Ollie Lovell) continues. Barton frames the issue around evidence-based teacher decision-making, from the theoretical (motivation mechanisms) to the highly practical (paper-folding tasks and daily routines).
points: Hendrick's summary of the Murayama/von Keyserlingk paper highlights its core critique: mainstream motivation theories (self-determination, expectancy-value, achievement goal theory) explain what motivates students without explaining how motivation is generated or sustained mechanistically.

The paper's proposed alternative -- a 'reward-learning framework' where awareness of a knowledge gap triggers information-seeking, which becomes rewarding and generates further questions -- reframes motivation as a self-sustaining cycle rather than a fixed trait to be boosted.

Rowlandson's paper-folding activity demonstrates how a single physical task can be re-posed across the full KS2-KS4 range, from identifying shape properties to proving why folds create specific angles.

Kane's Do Now routine -- five retrieval questions, three minutes flat, brief answer review, deeper follow-up deferred to later -- operationalizes the 'don't do too much, don't spend too much time' discipline Barton highlights as the piece's core lesson.
quotes: I am absolutely loving Carl's posts at the moment. This one on motivation is particularly good, distilling the research and sharing the key implications for classroom teachers.
One of my favourite bloggers is back - yay! Paul returns with a wonderful post about paper-folding and the mathematical questions we could ask students.
Regular listeners to my podcast will know that Ollie Lovell and I are on a Do Now deep-dive, so I enjoyed this post where Dylan shares his Do Now routine.
